analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Obama-era rule requiring retirement advisers to act in savers' best interest, replacing it with lighter disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved the bill 23-17 and it sat on the House calendar, but it never received a floor vote before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out the Department of Labor's 2016 "fiduciary rule," which required anyone giving retirement investment advice — including brokers selling rollovers and annuities into IRAs — to put the saver's interests first and exposed them to lawsuits if they did not. In its place, the bill writes a narrower statutory definition of advice and a "best interest recommendation" standard that allows commission-based sales and proprietary products as long as the adviser discloses them. The stated purpose is to keep advice affordable for small savers; the practical effect is to relieve financial firms of the strongest conflicts-of-interest requirements in the rule.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main winners would be broker-dealers, insurance agents selling annuities, and financial advisers paid by commission, who would no longer face the 2016 rule's requirement to serve savers' best interests or its private right of enforcement. The bill also helps advisers who said the rule's compliance costs would force them to stop serving small accounts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 2016 fiduciary rule and seven related prohibited-transaction exemptions, restoring the pre-2016 legal landscape for advice providers.

It replaces the rule with a narrower "best interest recommendation" standard that permits advisers to recommend a limited menu of options, including their own proprietary products, and to earn variable commissions, provided they give prescribed written disclosures and charge no more than reasonable compensation.

It gives advice providers a safe harbor: an accidental error or omission in the required disclosures does not create liability if corrected within 30 days, and savers' remedy for bad advice is generally limited to being paid back actual damages.

It carves large categories of communications out of the fiduciary definition entirely — sales and marketing pitches, platform providers, valuation information, and general financial education — so those communications carry no fiduciary duty at all.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, retirement savers — especially people rolling 401(k) balances into IRAs, where conflicted sales pitches are most common — would bear the cost through higher fees and products chosen for the seller's commission rather than the saver's return. The bill's compensation-disclosure regime relies on the saver reading and acting on the disclosures rather than a legal duty enforced against the adviser.

drawbacks.text: The bill's central weakness, acknowledged by its own supporters' framing, is that disclosure is a weaker protection than a fiduciary duty: savers would be handed written notices about variable compensation and limited product menus but would lose the rule's requirement that advice actually be in their best interest, enforceable against the adviser.

The industry's good-faith objection is real: the 2016 rule imposed significant compliance and liability costs, and industry groups argued this would push advisers to drop small and middle-income savers rather than serve them under the stricter standard — the concern the bill's title responds to.

The bill's own standard still imposes requirements — written acknowledgments, prescribed disclosures, a damages remedy — that some advice providers would have found burdensome, so it is not a pure win even for the industry it favors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a legally enforceable best-interest duty for disclosure paperwork. The honest case for it is cost and access: some advisers said the rule made small accounts unprofitable to serve. The honest case against it is that the conflicted-advice problem the rule targeted — commission-driven rollover and annuity sales — falls hardest on savers least equipped to evaluate disclosures, and the bill's remedy for bad advice is limited to repayment of actual damages. The savings-versus-protection tradeoff is real, but the bill resolves it decisively in the industry's favor.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee twice over, was discharged from the second committee, and was placed on the House calendar in March 2018 — but the House never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. David Roe introduced the bill on June 8, 2017; it was referred to the Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means Committees.
On July 19, 2017, the Education and the Workforce Committee ordered the bill reported as amended on a 23-17 vote, and reported it on October 25, 2017 (H. Rept. 115-371, Part I).
Ways and Means received three extensions of its referral before being discharged on March 5, 2018, when the bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 443 — the step before a floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred; the bill died on the calendar when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

The bill's main objective was partly accomplished by other means: in March 2018 the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the Department of Labor's fiduciary rule, and the Department ultimately abandoned its defense of the rule, so the pre-2016 landscape the bill sought largely arrived anyway without a new law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Retirement savers kept the fiduciary rule's protections on paper because the bill never became law, but the industry still largely got the outcome it wanted when courts vacated the rule in 2018 — so commission-based advice providers and annuity sellers came out ahead in practice, without needing the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The committee approved it 23-17 and all 30 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have freed them from the 2016 rule's best-interest duty on rollover and IRA advice, letting them keep commission-driven sales so long as they hand the saver prescribed disclosures. Their gain comes directly from weakening the protection savers would otherwise have.

The fiduciary rule covered annuity sales into retirement accounts, and one of the exemptions the bill nullifies specifically governs insurance agents and brokers. The bill would have restored the pre-2016 environment for these high-commission products.

industries.industry: Mutual fund and proprietary product distributors
industries.note: The bill's best-interest standard expressly allows recommending a limited menu including the seller's own products, with only a written notice that cheaper options may exist elsewhere — locking in shelf-space economics that a true fiduciary standard would discourage.
